content.p: In the second half of 1965 and into 1966, the Indonesian army and groups it worked with killed people in numbers that sources put anywhere from about 80,000 to 3 million, with about 500,000 the figure most often cited. The victims were mostly members and supporters of the Indonesian Communist Party, known as the PKI, and many others who were only accused of links to it. No official death toll has ever been issued, and according to POV none of the perpetrators has been convicted in a national or international court. The killings reshaped the country's politics for the next three decades under General Suharto, and their legacy remains contested in Indonesia.
content.h2: A failed coup and the army's answer
content.p: On the night of 30 September and 1 October 1965, a group calling itself the September 30th Movement abducted and killed six army generals. The POV background describes the group as dissident military officers and high-ranking PKI members. A radio announcement said the group had acted to protect President Sukarno from right-wing generals who were planning a coup. The Conversation reports that the bodies of the abducted men were later found in an old well at Lubang Buaya in east Jakarta. The Jakarta Post, in a 2016 report, gave the number of generals killed as seven, which differs from the other sources here.

Major General Suharto took control of the army leadership, cajoled and intimidated the movement's troops in central Jakarta into surrendering, and stormed its headquarters at the Halim air base. The Conversation says he defeated the movement in less than 48 hours. The army then blamed the PKI for the killings. Margaret Scott, writing in The New York Review of Books, reports that the group said it was forestalling a takeover by a CIA-backed "Council of Generals". Sources disagree on who ordered the generals' killing, and the 2017 declassified embassy files suggest that US officials received reports in November 1965 that the killing may have been an operation within the government, not a PKI plan.

The army's campaign against the PKI began in mid-October 1965. According to the POV documentary background, the army worked with local gangsters and anti-communist Muslim and student organizations. Those it targeted included ethnic Chinese, leftists, academics, trade unionists and artists. The Conversation describes the violence arriving in Central Java in the third week of October, moving to East Java in November, and reaching Bali in December. Special Forces units were sent to arrest, imprison and kill people suspected of PKI membership.

Human Rights First, reporting on the Komnas HAM findings, said that many victims had nothing to do with the party. It quoted the head of the Komnas HAM investigation, Nur Kholis, as saying that military officers made it appear that these people were linked to the PKI. Most victims were unarmed, were often taken from their homes in secret, were held as political prisoners and were then executed, according to POV.

Sukarno could not stop the killings. Under pressure from the military, he transferred emergency power to Suharto on 11 March 1966, and Suharto banned the PKI. He was appointed acting president by parliament in 1967 and then ruled as a military dictator until 1998, according to POV and The Conversation.
content.h2: Who was held and what Komnas HAM found
content.p: In July 2012 the National Human Rights Commission, Komnas HAM, published an 840-page report. The Jakarta Post reported that the commission declared the purge that followed the 1965 coup a gross violation of human rights. Its investigators said the killings were organised, systematic and widespread across the archipelago, except Papua. The report listed murder, slavery, forced disappearance, torture, rape and forced prostitution among the crimes it attributed to officials of Kopkamtib, the security command first led by Suharto.

The Jakarta Post summary said the report named Suharto and Kopkamtib officials as the most responsible for organising the purge. Human Rights First gave the investigation length as nearly three years, while Inside Indonesia described it as a four-year investigation. Both agree that it heard from 349 people. The commission did not give an official death toll. It did record specific mass killings: at least 300 people in Sragen, Central Java, at least 1,000 in Maumere, and 600 in Surabaya. It found at least 11,500 people forced into slavery on prison islands, including Buru and Moncong Loe, and about 41,000 forced to leave their homes.

Inside Indonesia reported that the commission's main conclusions covered violations between October 1965 and 1978, and that the commission found individual criminal responsibility among the military command, officers in control of troops, and personnel in the field. Komnas HAM recommended that the Attorney General investigate further, that a truth and reconciliation commission be set up, and that the president apologise to victims. Inside Indonesia said the report was the first time an official government body had said that crimes against humanity took place.

The United States role has been documented in two stages. In 1990, former US diplomats and CIA officers told The Seattle Times that the American embassy had compiled comprehensive lists of Communist Party officials, from top leaders down to village cadres, and had furnished as many as 5,000 names to the Indonesian army. The American officials later checked off the names of those who were killed or captured, they said. Robert Martens, a former member of the embassy's political section, told the paper: "They probably killed a lot of people, and I probably have a lot of blood on my hands." A CIA spokesman said there was "no substance" to the allegation that the agency was involved in preparing the list.

In 2017 the US government released about 30,000 pages of embassy files from Jakarta. The Financial Times, reporting on them, said officials tracked the killings closely and that the United States gave the Indonesian military money, equipment and lists of communist officials. The files also showed that US officials had credible information that contradicted the army's claim that the PKI had ordered the generals' killing. Bradley Simpson, the historian who led the digitisation, said the Indonesian government had not released most of its own records from the period.

No official figure exists. The Journal of Asian Studies published a 2017 study that describes a consensus estimate of approximately 500,000 deaths. It also says earlier estimates had been drawn exclusively from anecdotal accounts, and it uses census data and demographic analysis, with East Java as a case study. The article does not apportion responsibility among the perpetrators.

Other figures are lower or higher. The Seattle Times reported an estimate of 250,000 lives, and The Seattle Times also reported that a CIA study from 1968 placed the dead at 250,000 and ranked the slaughter among the gravest mass killings of the century. The Conversation gives a range of 200,000 to 800,000. Human Rights First cited an estimate of 500,000 with some estimates as high as one million. POV says the army killed an estimated 500,000, and perhaps as many as one million, over about six months.

The Jakarta Post's 2016 report on a national symposium showed the official dispute. Coordinating Minister Luhut Pandjaitan said the government would not apologise, citing a lack of evidence. He said he did not believe the number was more than 1,000, probably less. Retired general Sintong Panjaitan said that Sukarno had set up an inquiry under former home minister Soemarno, and that by December 1965 its members had reported around 80,000 dead. The Jakarta Post also reported that the upper figure of 3 million had once been boastingly cited by Sarwo Edhie Wibowo, who headed the Army's Special Forces during the campaign. Reza Muharam, of an international people's tribunal on the events, called Sintong's figure a gross underestimate.

For decades the government barred publications that mentioned the 1965-66 events in the name of public order, and school textbooks called the crackdown an act of patriotism. Human Rights First says this ban was lifted only in 2010. Inside Indonesia reports that the 2012 Komnas HAM findings were welcomed by most survivors and rights advocates. The day after the report was released, a meeting in Bandung of veterans' groups and Golkar politicians rejected it, arguing that it had not considered the violence of the PKI. General Solihin, a former governor of West Java, rejected a proposed presidential apology and a human rights court.

Inside Indonesia said the report had provoked wide debate and had changed the language used by much of the mainstream press. It also said the new information was unlikely to bring about political or legal change, because elites who benefited from the killings still held overwhelming political and ideological control. Human Rights First quoted KontraS, a rights group, as saying the attorney general's office had a record of neglecting other gross violation cases.

On 11 January 2023 President Joko Widodo acknowledged a series of incidents amounting to gross human rights violations, including the bloodshed and arrests of 1965 and 1966. Reuters, reporting through TimesLive, said he cited 11 other incidents between 1965 and 2003. He said that "with a clear genuine mind and conscience" he acknowledged gross violations had occurred, and that the government would restore victims' rights "fairly and wisely without negating judicial resolving". He did not say how. TimesLive reported that earlier presidents had also acknowledged the events: the late Abdurrahman Wahid apologised for the 1965 bloodshed, and BJ Habibie formed a team to investigate in 1998.

Activists were not satisfied. Usman Hamid of Amnesty International, quoted by TimesLive, said serious crimes of the past needed to be resolved through judicial means and that victims needed reparation. Those who suffered in 1965 still carry the consequences: former political prisoners had their identity cards marked, and their children were barred from civil service and the military, according to The Conversation.
